Why are customers in Texas underspending compared to California?

text:
**Texas customers are not underspending—they actually spend 6.1% more per customer than Californians ($125.97 vs. $118.74); the total revenue gap is entirely driven by having 32% fewer customers.**

| Metric | California | Texas | Variance (TX vs. CA) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Total Net Revenue** | $292,572.91 | $211,132.76 | -27.8% (-$81,440.15) |
| **Purchasing Customers** | 2,464 | 1,676 | -32.0% (-788 customers) |
| **Registered User Base** | 3,696 | 2,481 | -32.9% (-1,215 users) |
| **Spend per Customer** | $118.74 | $125.97 | **+6.1% (+$7.23)** |
| **Orders per Customer** | 1.41 | 1.44 | +2.1% (+0.03 orders) |
| **Average Item Value** | $59.05 | $60.90 | +3.1% (+$1.85) |
| **Items per Order** | 1.43 | 1.43 | Flat |

*(Note: Net revenue excludes cancelled and returned items across all time. Metric decomposition: Spend per Customer = Orders per Customer × Items per Order × Avg Item Value.)*

- **The premise contradicts customer behavior:** When decomposed into orders per customer (1.44 vs. 1.41) and average item price ($60.90 vs. $59.05), an individual Texan buyer generates more lifetime revenue than an individual Californian buyer.
- **The true driver is customer acquisition volume:** California generates $81.4k more total revenue solely because it has 1,215 more registered accounts (3,696 vs. 2,481), matching the broader state population disparity; conversion rates from sign-up to purchase are essentially identical (TX: 67.6% vs. CA: 66.7%).
- **Actionable next step:** Regional marketing should treat Texas as a high-yield customer acquisition opportunity rather than an under-monetized basket problem, reallocating top-of-funnel acquisition ad spend toward Texas where customer value is proven higher.
